### SC4N-CODE-TAINT-SHELL

**Data from an untrusted source reaches a shell or process sink** · severity `critical` · confidence `medium` · class `code` · [CWE-78](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/78.html)

A value derived from an external source is passed to os.system, os.popen, os.exec*/os.spawn*, subprocess.*, pty.spawn or commands.getoutput. Builder-style APIs that pass an argument vector are still reported, because the vector element is only one quoting mistake away from a shell; `shell=True` is recorded in the finding's extra fields when it is written next to the call.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/78.html


### SC4N-CODE-TAINT-TEMPLATE

**Data from an untrusted source is rendered as a template** · severity `high` · confidence `medium` · class `code` · [CWE-1336](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1336.html)

Jinja2 from_string/from_file is called with a template string derived from an external source (a chat template, a metadata value, a downloaded config). Untrusted template source is server-side template injection; the Jinja analyser in internal/jinja reads the template's own contents, while this rule fires on the code path that would render it.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1336.html


### SC4N-CONFIG-ARCHITECTURE-UNKNOWN

**config.json names an architecture outside the known Transformers set** · severity `info` · confidence `low` · class `config` · [CWE-1357](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1357.html)

A `config.json` `architectures` entry is not one of the model classes Transformers ships. That is frequently an ordinary custom or brand-new architecture, but a class name the local library does not know is also what routes loading through a repository-provided module (see SC4N-CONFIG-AUTO-MAP). Informational: the name is recorded so a reviewer can check whether it resolves to a library the user already has.

References:

- https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/main_classes/model


### SC4N-CONFIG-AUTO-MAP

**config.json selects a local module to import and execute** · severity `critical` · confidence `high` · class `config` · [CWE-502](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/502.html), [CWE-94](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/94.html)

A Hugging Face config carries an `auto_map`, which maps an Auto* class (AutoConfig, AutoModel, AutoTokenizer, …) to a Python module and class name inside the repository. With trust_remote_code enabled the loader imports that module and executes it, so the model file itself is code. The finding is one per referenced repository, not one per entry: seven Auto* classes that resolve to the same module package are one decision to load it, and the evidence states how many entries were folded and which classes they name. For a module inside the repository the finding also states whether sc4n found the matching .py file in the scanned tree (a local module is code that will run; a module that is absent still fails the same way at load time). This is the VU#456290 / CVE-2026-4372 surface. Critical because an auto_map is code execution on the artifact's normal load path.

References:

- https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/main_classes/model#models-hosted-on-the-hub
- https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/456290
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-4372


### SC4N-CONFIG-CHAT-TEMPLATE

**config carries a chat template, which the Jinja2 rules analysed** · severity `info` · confidence `high` · class `config` · [CWE-1336](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1336.html)

A config.json or tokenizer_config.json carries a `chat_template`. The field may be a single string, a list of {name, template} objects, or an object keyed by name; sc4n extracts every entry and hands each one to the Jinja2 analyser (SC4N-JINJA-* and SC4N-TEMPLATE-INJECTION), because a scanner that reads only the first list entry misses a malicious second one. Informational: it exists so the report shows how many templates were seen and under which names. The template itself is the attack surface for chat-template SSTI (CVE-2026-5760 / CERT VU#915947).

References:

- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-5760
- https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/915947


### SC4N-CONFIG-TRUST-REMOTE-CODE

**config.json enables trust_remote_code** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `config` · [CWE-502](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/502.html), [CWE-94](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/94.html)

A Hugging Face config sets `trust_remote_code` to a truthful value. That flag is an explicit instruction to the loader to import and execute Python from the repository (the `auto_map` modules, custom tokenizers, custom configuration classes), so setting it is a decision to run untrusted code. High rather than critical because the flag alone only permits code execution; it needs a co-located module to actually run, and sc4n reports the `auto_map` separately with SC4N-CONFIG-AUTO-MAP.

References:

- https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/security
- https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/456290


### SC4N-JINJA-DANGEROUS-GLOBAL

**Template walks an attribute off a Jinja2 global that reaches __globals__** · severity `high` · confidence `medium` · class `template` · [CWE-1336](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1336.html)

A Jinja2 template uses one of the globals that immediately reaches an interesting object as the receiver of an attribute or subscript access: lipsum, cycler, joiner, namespace, dict or range, or it applies the `attr` filter to a name that starts with an underscore. lipsum.__globals__['os'].popen(…) and cycler.__init__.__globals__ are the canonical chains, and they exist because these globals are real Python objects whose __globals__ is the template module's namespace. The bare constructors themselves (namespace(a=1), dict(...), range(3)) are ordinary template style and are not reported by this rule; the finding is the attribute access out of them. (A computed {% set ns = namespace(...) %} is separately a low-confidence SC4N-JINJA-DYNAMIC-NAME, not a gadget.)

References:

- https://portswigger.net/web-security/server-side-template-injection
- https://hacktricks.wiki/en/pentesting-web/ssti-server-side-template-injection/


### SC4N-JINJA-DYNAMIC-NAME

**Template assembles a name or value instead of writing it literally** · severity `medium` · confidence `low` · class `template` · [CWE-1336](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1336.html), [CWE-506](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html)

A Jinja2 template builds a string by concatenation (the classic '__g' + 'lobals__' that defeats a name denylist), applies the `attr` filter to a computed name, or assigns a value with {% set %} whose right-hand side is computed rather than a literal, a name or a filter chain. None of these is proof of intent on its own, which is why the confidence is low; the constructive form is reported because obfuscating an introspection name is the first thing a template-injection payload has to do.

References:

- https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Code_Injection
- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1336.html


### SC4N-JINJA-INCLUDE

**Template loads another template or module file** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `template` · [CWE-1336](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1336.html)

A Jinja2 template uses {% include %}, {% import %}, {% extends %} or {% from %}, so rendering it reads another file that the loader resolves (and, in Jinja's own examples, can build the name from a variable). A chat template shipped with a model has no reason to pull in a sibling file; when one does, the sibling is part of the artifact's executable surface and is only safe if it was scanned too.

References:

- https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/templates/#import
- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1336.html


### SC4N-JINJA-PY-OBJECT

**Template reaches a Python object through a dunder attribute or name** · severity `critical` · confidence `high` · class `template` · [CWE-1336](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1336.html), [CWE-94](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/94.html)

A Jinja2 template contains an attribute, subscript or name from the Python introspection set: __class__, __mro__, __subclasses__, __globals__, __builtins__, __import__, __init__, __reduce__, __getattribute__, __dict__, __code__ or __loader__. Jinja2 is not sandboxed, so walking from any value to one of these reaches an arbitrary callable: __class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()[i]\(...) is the standard chain, and the `attr` filter (|attr('__globals__')) reaches the same names through a string. This is the class behind CVE-2026-5760 (SGLang /v1/rerank, CVSS 9.8) and CERT VU#915947. A chat template has no legitimate reason to name any of them.

References:

- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-5760
- https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/915947
- https://portswigger.net/web-security/server-side-template-injection


### SC4N-JINJA-RAW

**Template hides a region inside a {% raw %} block** · severity `low` · confidence `high` · class `template` · [CWE-1336](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1336.html)

A Jinja2 template contains a {% raw %} (or {% verbatim %}) block. Everything inside is emitted literally, so a scanner that tokenises {{ }} and {% %} sees the delimiters but not the content. A real chat template rarely needs one, and a payload that wants its own delimiters to survive into the prompt uses exactly this. Low severity because the technique is also used legitimately to show template syntax in documentation.

References:

- https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/templates/#escaping


### SC4N-MODULES-REMOTE-MODULE

**sentence-transformers modules.json reconstructs a remote module stack** · severity `medium` · confidence `low` · class `modules` · [CWE-829](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html)

A sentence-transformers `modules.json` has an entry whose `path` is a URL, an absolute path, or a relative path that walks out of the repository, so loading the model fetches a module the scan did not read and composes it with the local ones. An empty path is NOT this rule's subject: entry 0 of every published sentence-transformers repository is the top-level Transformer with `path: ""`, meaning the repository root itself. Severity is medium and confidence low because the remote module may be a legitimate published stack; the finding's value is naming the module type that comes from somewhere else.

References:

- https://sbert.net/docs/package_reference/sentence_transformer/models.html
- https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/security


### SC4N-TEMPLATE-INJECTION

**Template embeds an instruction that overrides the conversation, with a channel to carry it out** · severity `high` · confidence `medium` · class `template` · [CWE-1426](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1426.html), [CWE-94](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/94.html)

A Jinja2 template carries an instruction aimed at the model rather than at a renderer — "ignore previous instructions", "do not tell the user", "system prompt:", "exfiltrate", a request to send the conversation elsewhere — *and* something in the same template that gives the instruction somewhere to go: a C2/webhook or raw-IP URL, a hidden HTML comment, an invisible-character run, or a base64 blob of at least 64 characters. A chat template is pasted into every conversation the model serves, so an instruction in it is a standing prompt injection (OWASP LLM01) and, with a channel to carry the result out, a backdoor. The corroboration requirement is what separates that from an ordinary tool-use sentence; the phrase-only case is SC4N-TEMPLATE-INJECTION-WEAK. The table deliberately excludes chat pseudo-tags like [INST] and <|im_start|>, which legitimate templates are built from, and the arguments of raise_exception(), which Transformers itself provides. High where SC4N-CARD-INJECTION is medium for the same phrasing: a card is read once, while a template is rendered around every conversation the model serves.

References:

- https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/
- https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/915947


### SC4N-TEMPLATE-INJECTION-WEAK

**Template contains model-directed instruction text (no channel corroborates it)** · severity `low` · confidence `low` · class `template` · [CWE-1426](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1426.html)

A Jinja2 template contains a phrase that is aimed at a model rather than at a renderer, and nothing else in the template corroborates it: no C2/webhook or raw-IP URL, no hidden HTML comment, no invisible-character run, no base64 blob. Reported because the phrase is in the artifact's executable surface, at low severity because a legitimate tool-use instruction reads the same way — "do not tell the user about function calls" is how three of llama.cpp's shipped templates put it. Read the matched phrase before concluding; the high-severity SC4N-TEMPLATE-INJECTION is the form with a channel.

References:

- https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/

## Containers, members and what stopped the walk

How to act on these: [`docs/triage.md#containers`](triage.md#containers).

### SC4N-ARCHIVE-CRC

**Archive member CRC-32 does not match its content** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `archive` · [CWE-354](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/354.html)

The member's bytes do not hash to the CRC-32 recorded in the directory. Either the archive is corrupt or it was edited after it was written, which is the shape a scanner using a reader that validates CRC (and a loader that does not) would disagree about.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/354.html


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-DIRECTORY-AMBIGUOUS

**Zip has two valid central directories** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `archive` · [CWE-436](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html)

The literal directory offset and the offset derived from the prefix both hold a central-directory signature, at different positions. A reader that resolves the prefix one way and a loader that resolves it another read different member sets, so a clean scan of this member list is not a clean statement about what the loader sees.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-DUPLICATE-NAME

**Archive contains duplicate member names** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `archive` · [CWE-436](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html)

Two members have the same name. Extractor behaviour then decides which copy wins: a scanner may scan the first and a loader may use the last, so the artifact is not what the scan described.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-ENCRYPTED

**Archive member is encrypted and cannot be inspected** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `archive` · [CWE-693](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/693.html)

The member is encrypted, so sc4n cannot read its content and the payload behind the encryption was not analysed. This is reported rather than skipped because an encrypted member is indistinguishable from a member whose scan failed: both mean "not analysed", never "clean".

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/693.html


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-LINK

**Archive contains a link or device member** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `archive` · [CWE-59](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/59.html)

The archive declares a symbolic link, a hard link or a device node. Extracting it creates a filesystem object whose target is chosen by the artifact rather than by the scanner, which is the link-following primitive used to read or overwrite files outside the extraction root (CWE-59). The link target is recorded in the evidence where the format carries it.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/59.html


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-MEMBER-ERROR

**Archive member could not be read** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `archive` · [CWE-755](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/755.html)

A member's structure is malformed or its data is corrupt, so its content was not analysed. A zip walk continues past the member (fail-closed iteration), so the rest of that archive was still scanned; a tar walk cannot, because a tar is a forward stream and a header that cannot be read ends the archive — so for a tar this finding means the members after it were not visited either. The member itself is reported as not analysed rather than silently skipped. modelscan issue #354 is exactly this: an unreadable entry before archive/data.pkl made the whole scan report CLEAN.

References:

- https://github.com/protectai/modelscan/issues/354


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-MEMBER-SKIPPED

**Archive member was not analysed** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `structure` · [CWE-1059](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1059.html)

A member was not dispatched to any parser: its typeflag is not a regular file, directory, link, device or fifo (a GNU sparse or contiguous member, or a type sc4n does not know), or its name is empty. The member's bytes were therefore not scanned by anything but the universal head/tail windows, and a payload can sit in the parts of it those windows do not cover. The finding names the typeflag so the reader can see what the archive claimed.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1059.html


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-NAME-MISMATCH

**Zip local header disagrees with the central directory** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `archive` · [CWE-436](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html)

A member's local file header and its central-directory record disagree about its name, compression method, CRC-32 or sizes. A reader that trusts one record and a loader that trusts the other see two different files — the classic way to show a scanner a benign member and load a hostile one — and a method disagreement means the bytes sc4n read are not the bytes a loader would decompress. The same rule reports a stored member whose central record declares different compressed and uncompressed sizes, which cannot both be true.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-NATIVE-MEMBER

**Archive contains a native executable member** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `executable` · [CWE-506](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html)

A member's bytes validate as an ELF, PE, Mach-O or ar executable. A model archive has no legitimate reason to carry native code, and the code runs as soon as anything executes the member. High rather than critical: loading the model does not run it, so unlike a pickle REDUCE there is no code execution on the normal load path — the same calibration the other native-in-container rules use (SC4N-POLYGLOT-NATIVE, SC4N-TFLITE-NATIVE-MAGIC, SC4N-NATIVE-EMBEDDED-PAYLOAD).

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-NESTED-COMPRESSION

**Compressed payload is wrapped in a second compression layer** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `archive` · [CWE-409](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/409.html)

A payload decompressed cleanly and is itself compressed. sc4n recurses through supported wrappers, but double wrapping is the published modelscan bypass (gzip of bzip2 of a pickle) because a scanner that decompresses one layer and then classifies the result sees compressed bytes, not a pickle. The finding records the inner algorithm.

References:

- https://github.com/protectai/modelscan/issues/354


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-PATH

**Archive member name is an absolute or traversal path** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `archive` · [CWE-22](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html)

A member name is absolute, contains a '..' segment, a NUL byte, a backslash separator, a Windows drive letter, or is longer than 4096 bytes. A loader that extracts without normalising the name writes or reads outside the destination directory (zip_slip). sc4n never extracts a member, so this is reported at the point the name is read, not at extraction time.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-SHEBANG

**Archive member is an executable script** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `executable` · [CWE-78](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/78.html)

A member starts with a '#!' interpreter line, so it is a script that becomes executable when extracted with its mode bits intact. sc4n does not execute it; it reports the interpreter name so the reader can see what the artifact intended to run.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/78.html


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-TRAILING-DATA

**Bytes follow the end-of-central-directory record** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `structure` · [CWE-436](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html)

The zip's end-of-central-directory record does not end at the end of the file: a region follows it. Appending bytes after the EOCD is the standard polyglot technique, and the appended region is invisible to a reader that trusts the central directory while a reader that scans the whole file sees it, so two tools can disagree about what the artifact contains. sc4n still walks the central directory (the members it describes are analysed), and reports the byte count so the appended region can be examined.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-TRUNCATED

**Zip has no central directory; members were recovered from local headers** · severity `info` · confidence `high` · class `format`

The file begins with zip local file headers but carries no end-of-central-directory record, which is what a 2 MiB header slice of a torch checkpoint looks like. sc4n walked the local headers forward and scanned every member they bound, so the findings under this artifact come from the part of the archive that is present. Members after the last header are not reachable and a member whose data descriptor is missing is bounded by the next header.


### SC4N-ARCHIVE-UNSUPPORTED-COMPRESSION

**Compression is recognised but cannot be decompressed** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `archive` · [CWE-693](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/693.html)

The bytes are wrapped in a compression algorithm for which the Go standard library has no decoder (xz, lzma, lz4, zstd, 7z, rar). sc4n does not shell out to a decompressor, so the payload inside was NOT scanned. The algorithm and the offset are named in the evidence. A 7z file named .pt is the February 2025 Hugging Face campaign: the loader still deserialised it while every extension-driven scanner saw "not a zip".

References:

- https://huggingface.co/blog/notable-models-scanned


### SC4N-NATIVE-EMBEDDED-PAYLOAD

**Native artifact embeds a second validated executable** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `native` · [CWE-506](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html)

A second complete native header was found inside a native artifact. The header was validated with Go's own executable-header parser, so this is a program embedded in a program, not bytes that happen to match a magic. Legitimate linkers do not append a second executable to their output, so the shape indicates a self-extracting or dropper payload carried inside an otherwise ordinary-looking binary. sc4n reports the offset; it does not extract or run anything.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html


### SC4N-NATIVE-EXEC-IMPORTS

**Native executable imports process-control symbols** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `executable` · [CWE-506](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html)

A validated ELF imports system, popen, an exec* variant, fork, dlopen or ptrace in its dynamic symbol table. sc4n does not disassemble the binary: these are the names the dynamic loader will bind when it is loaded, which is the loader's own statement that the program can spawn a shell, execute a file or open another process's memory. A C extension that merely does arithmetic imports none of them, so the set separates a numerical library from a dropper. It is high rather than critical for the same reason SC4N-POLYGLOT-NATIVE is: loading the model does not run the member.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html


### SC4N-NATIVE-VALID

**Artifact is a validated native executable** · severity `info` · confidence `high` · class `native`

The artifact is a native executable whose header was accepted by Go's debug/elf, debug/macho or debug/pe parser (ar archives and OLE compound files use the structural check in internal/bytescan). sc4n does not disassemble or run it; the finding records that the bytes are a program, which is the honest baseline for a repository that expects to ship weights. A native binary inside a model artifact is worth an explicit decision, particularly when it arrives as an archive member rather than a declared dependency.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html


### SC4N-PARSE-FAILED

**Format parser could not walk the artifact to the end** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `structure` · [CWE-755](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/755.html)

The parser for this artifact's sniffed format returned an error part-way through, so whatever lies past that point was not analysed. This is reported as a finding rather than as a silent skip because a truncated walk is the classic way to make a scanner report CLEAN: modelscan issue #354 is an unreadable ZIP entry placed before archive/data.pkl. Read the evidence for the failing structure and treat the artifact as unscanned beyond that point.

References:

- https://github.com/protectai/modelscan/issues/354


### SC4N-PATH-ESCAPE

**Reference resolves outside the scan root** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `path` · [CWE-22](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html), [CWE-59](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/59.html)

A path-shaped value was resolved with os.Root and rejected because it leaves the containment root (through '..', an absolute name, or a symlink whose target is outside). sc4n never opens the file in that case; the finding tells the reviewer that the artifact asked for a path it is not allowed to read, which is the same request an arbitrary-file-read exploit makes.

References:

- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-25882


### SC4N-POLYGLOT-CONTAINER

**Artifact is more than one container format** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `polyglot` · [CWE-436](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html)

Two container signatures occupy their canonical anchors in one file: a leading magic at offset 0 (zip, 7z, rar, gzip, bzip2, xz, lz4, zstd or HDF5) together with the tar ustar anchor at offset 257. A file both a zip and a tar is the classic container polyglot: two different readers open it two different ways, so a scanner that only knows one container never sees what the other one loads. sc4n reports the coexistence, not a loadability proof, because the second container's checksum is not validated here.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyglot_(computing)


### SC4N-POLYGLOT-MAGIC-ONLY

**Native magic signature without a valid header** · severity `info` · confidence `medium` · class `polyglot` · [CWE-436](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html)

The artifact carries a native-executable magic (ELF, PE/DOS, Mach-O, ar, OLE or an APE sigil) but the validation for that kind rejects it — debug/elf, debug/macho and debug/pe for the first three, the structural check in internal/bytescan for ar, OLE and an APE whose PE header does not parse — so the magic is data that looks like a header rather than a loadable program. Reported at info because a four-byte match is common in binary tensor data; it is the validated match (SC4N-POLYGLOT-NATIVE) that means code. A leading magic that does not validate is also how a truncated or deliberately malformed executable is disguised as a model.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html


### SC4N-POLYGLOT-NATIVE

**Validated native executable embedded in a non-native artifact** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `polyglot` · [CWE-506](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html), [CWE-436](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html)

A complete native executable header (ELF, PE/DOS, Mach-O, an ar object archive or an OLE compound file) was found inside an artifact that was dispatched as something else. The header was validated — by Go's own debug/elf, debug/macho or debug/pe parser for those three, and by the structural check in internal/bytescan for an ar object archive and an OLE compound file, for which the standard library has no parser at all — so this is real code, not four bytes that happen to match a magic. Nothing in sc4n executes it; the finding is the statement that the file carries a program alongside the model, which is the shape both a malicious repository and a self-extracting single-file model (an APE/llamafile is exactly this) present to a loader.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html
- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/436.html
- https://huggingface.co/blog/notable-models-scanned
- https://justine.lol/ape.html


### SC4N-POLYGLOT-SHEBANG

**Binary artifact begins with an interpreter directive** · severity `info` · confidence `medium` · class `polyglot` · [CWE-506](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html)

The artifact's first two bytes are "#!", so the file is a script, not the binary container or model its content was dispatched as. The rule is suppressed for text-like formats (Python, notebook, Jinja, Markdown, YAML, JSON, plain text) where a shebang is idiomatic; it reports the contradiction case, where a shell or interpreter line sits at the head of bytes that were otherwise identified as a model artifact.

References:

- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html

## Model formats and graph semantics

How to act on these: [`docs/triage.md#model-graphs`](triage.md#model-graphs).

### SC4N-COREML-CUSTOM-LAYER

**Core ML model names a host-supplied custom class** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `format` · [CWE-829](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html), [CWE-494](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/494.html)

A CustomModel (ModelProto field 555) or a NeuralNetwork layer's CustomLayerParams (field 500) declares a className. The model file contains no implementation of that class: Core ML asks the host application to supply one that conforms to MLCustomModel/MLCustomLayer and to register it under that name. Loading the file therefore reaches whatever the host resolves the name to. A poisoned package pairs with a host plugin, and the model itself can look like ordinary weights, so the finding is about the pairing rather than the bytes.

References:

- https://apple.github.io/coremltools/mlmodel/Format/Model.html
- https://developer.apple.com/documentation/coreml/mlcustommodel


### SC4N-COREML-PROGRAM-UNVERIFIED

**Core ML ML Program graph is not decoded** · severity `info` · confidence `high` · class `format`

Model.type is `mlProgram` (MILSpec.Program, field 502), the modern Core ML graph representation. sc4n v1 recognises it but does not decode the MIL operator graph or its weight blobs, so this model is reported as only shallowly analysed rather than silently treated as clean. Custom layers named by an ML Program are not covered by SC4N-COREML-CUSTOM-LAYER.


### SC4N-COREML-STRUCT

**Core ML model is structurally invalid or only partly walked** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `format` · [CWE-20](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/20.html)

The protobuf could not be walked as a ModelProto: a field tag, length or fixed value was truncated or malformed, a protobuf group wire type was used, or the model is larger than the bounded walk window so only its head was inspected. Every length is validated by protowire before use, so nothing is allocated from an attacker-controlled size; the finding tells the reviewer that the declared Core ML structure and sc4n disagree about the document.

References:

- https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/encoding/


### SC4N-GGUF-ENDIAN-AMBIGUOUS

**GGUF version 3 byte order is ambiguous; one was chosen** · severity `info` · confidence `low` · class `structure` · [CWE-20](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/20.html)

GGUF version 3 added a big-endian variant and the format carries no flag that names the byte order, so a reader has to infer it. sc4n tested the declared counts (and the first metadata key length) under both orders; when both are plausible, or only big-endian is, it reports this finding and states which order it used rather than guessing silently. A file whose counts are plausible in both orders cannot be interpreted unambiguously by sc4n; the evidence names the order this parse used, so the tensor geometry reported alongside it belongs to that reading and not necessarily to the one a loader would choose.

References:

- https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md


### SC4N-GGUF-EXTENT-UNVERIFIED

**GGUF tensor extent could not be computed; geometry checks skipped** · severity `info` · confidence `high` · class `structure`

A tensor names a ggml type whose block size sc4n cannot confirm, or an element count that is not a whole number of blocks, so its byte extent is unknown. sc4n deliberately skips the overlap, alignment-of-end and trailing-data checks for it: a wrong block size would fabricate an overlap or a trailing payload, and a false "trailing data" finding is worse than an honest "not verified". The tensor's own offset alignment is still checked.

References:

- https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md


### SC4N-GGUF-POLYGLOT

**GGUF carries an APE/llamafile sigil or an embedded native executable** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `structure` · [CWE-506](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html)

An APE sigil (MZqFpD=' or jartsr=') or a validated ELF/PE/Mach-O header appears in the first 8 KiB or the last 1 MiB of the file. This is the llamafile single-file-executable shape: one file that is both a model and a runnable program, so a tool that treats it as weights and a person who runs it as a binary see different things. Executables are validated with the standard library's debug/elf, debug/macho and debug/pe header parsers; a bare magic match without a valid header is left to the format-independent polyglot layer at info.

References:

- https://github.com/Mozilla-Ocho/llamafile
- https://justine.lol/ape.html


### SC4N-GGUF-STRUCT

**GGUF structure violates the format's own header** · severity `medium` · confidence `high` · class `structure` · [CWE-20](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/20.html)

The file's declared counts, key or tensor metadata contradict the bytes actually present: absent magic, a version outside {2,3}, a count larger than the file, an illegal key or tensor-name length, a duplicate metadata key, a retired or out-of-range ggml type, more than four dimensions, a zero dimension, a tensor offset that is misaligned, out of declaration order or overlapping its predecessor, or a tensor extent that runs past EOF. A run of extents past EOF — what a truncated download or a header slice is — is one event, so the first such tensor is reported by name and extent and the rest are reported once, as an aggregate naming how many further extents run past EOF and where the first and last of them end. These are exactly the checks the llama.cpp GGUF reader performs, and the parser bugs that reached CVEs (CVE-2024-21802, CVE-2024-23496, CVE-2024-23605, CVE-2025-53630 cumulative-size overflow, CVE-2026-33298 ggml_nbytes overflow, GHSA-8wwf-w4qm-gpqr) were triggered by count/offset arithmetic on values like these. A reader that accepts this file is reading a different byte layout than the one the header describes.

References:

- https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-21802
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-53630
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-33298
- https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/security/advisories/GHSA-8wwf-w4qm-gpqr


### SC4N-GGUF-TRAILING-DATA

**GGUF has undeclared trailing data after the last tensor** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `structure` · [CWE-506](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html)

The file is longer than 8 + metadata + aligned tensor region + the last tensor's extent, so bytes exist that no tensor describes. The GGUF reader never looks at them, which is what makes the shape useful for smuggling: a second artifact can live there and every GGUF-only tool reports a normal model. The evidence carries the residual length, its byte entropy and any validated native magic found in it.

References:

- https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md

A node or opset import names a domain outside the ONNX-defined sets, so the operator it binds to (or the whole op set it imports) has to be provided by a native extension of the runtime. ### SC4N-ONNX-EXTERNAL-BOUNDS

**ONNX external_data offset/length is out of bounds** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `resource` · [CWE-190](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/190.html), [CWE-400](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/400.html)

external_data carries 'offset' and 'length' as decimal strings. This finding means the value is not a non-negative decimal integer (a negative, hexadecimal or non-numeric value), is petabyte-scale (>= 1 PiB, far above any published model and enough to overflow an allocation computed from it), or runs past the end of the file it names. The hardened loader accepts exactly {location, offset, length, checksum, basepath} in external_data and rejects everything else. An out-of-whitelist key is either a typo the loader will ignore or, when it is a dunder name such as '__class__' or '__reduce__', input to a setattr-shaped sink that overwrites a protocol attribute instead of a data field. That is the attribute-injection half of CVE-2026-34445 = GHSA-538c-55jv-c5g9 (not CVE-2026-34447, which is the path-handling bug GHSA-p433-9wv8-28xj).

The referenced external tensor file exists and is a symbolic link (or has a symlinked final component). ModelProto.functions is non-empty, or a node carries an 'overload' value. The protobuf structure contradicts the ONNX specification: a missing ir_version, graph or opset_import, a field whose wire type cannot be the declared ONNX type, a negative dimension, a data_type of UNDEFINED, raw_data whose length does not equal product(dims) x element size, external_data that is not marked with data_location=EXTERNAL, or both raw_data and external_data set. ### SC4N-PTE-NATIVE

**Native executable embedded in ExecuTorch segment data** · severity `high` · confidence `high` · class `polyglot` · [CWE-506](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/506.html)

A validated ELF/PE/Mach-O header was found inside the segment region the extended header declares. The runtime maps that region and hands it to the device backend, and the universal polyglot layer only inspects the first and last MiB of a file, so an executable positioned in the middle of a large segment region would otherwise go unseen. The header was validated with the standard library's own parser, so this is a real image and not four coincidental bytes.

The `.pte` header does not satisfy its own layout: the file magic is not `ET` plus two ASCII digits at offset 4, the flatbuffer root offset points outside the file, or the optional extended header's declared size, program-data size or segment region is out of range. A loader that trusts these fields reads a different byte range than sc4n inspected, so a malformed header is treated as a mismatch rather than a parse detail.

### SC4N-PTE-UNVERIFIED

**ExecuTorch program is recognised but not deep-parsed** · severity `info` · confidence `high` · class `format`

The file has a valid ExecuTorch `.pte` header (flatbuffer root offset plus the `ET` file magic at offset 4), but sc4n v1 does not decode the flatbuffer program graph or the operator set it references. Those operators are native code on the device, so the file's behaviour is decided by the runtime the device ships. This finding exists so that a clean report on a `.pte` is read as "recognised, shallowly analysed" rather than "analysed and safe".

References:

- https://docs.pytorch.org/executorch/stable/pte-file-format.html
